CENTRAL BANK OF NICARAGUA
Nicaragua
Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than they were worth and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is put at 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by the bank's president, Ovidio Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.

CENTRAL BANK OF ARUBA
Aruba
The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the Aruban florin and holds it at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its Central Bank Ordinance of 1991, amended through 2014, keeps the bank under the Governor of Aruba and the Minister of Finance. Section 18 has the Governor appoint the president and executive directors from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board, and suspend or dismiss them by state decree; section 19(3) allows general guidelines for their duties to be set by decree; section 23 gives him the appointment and dismissal of the supervisory directors; and section 27(1) has the Government Commissioner supervise the bank under the Minister's instructions. One case is recorded: the General Audit Chamber, reviewing the country's 2001-2004 accounts, found contributions paid into an earmarked account at the bank for the Fondo Desaroyo Aruba foundation were not accounted for completely, correctly and on time, with 16,898,503 florins paid in by the Netherlands left off the balance sheet out of a 19.3 million florin balance at the end of 2000. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied new banknotes in 2019, on a client list in another organisation's announcement rather than a contract notice, so that is reported rather than confirmed by the bank. BNP Paribas Asset Management runs a fixed income mandate in US dollars and gives advice, and Ernst & Young audits the accounts. Aruba scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. CENTRAL BANK OF SYRIA
Syria
The Central Bank of Syria issues the Syrian pound, which moves within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Basic Monetary Law No. 23 of 2002, issued in Damascus on 17 March 2002 by President Bashar al-Assad, places the bank and its policy-making council under the government. Article 1 has the Monetary and Credit Council work within the general economic directions of the state approved by the Council of Ministers. Article 8(3) has its decisions passed to the Minister of Economy and Foreign Trade, who may suspend for up to seven days any decision he considers contrary to the interest of the state and must refer a continuing disagreement to the Council of Ministers. Article 69 has the Governor appointed, and his service ended, by decree; article 2 puts the Council's non-bank seats, among them assistant ministers and the head of the State Planning Authority, in the gift of a decree; and article 71 has the Minister name the four supervising directors who sit with the Governor on the management committee. Government pressure was reported in 11 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time pressing the bank to ease and demanding that it print money. One case runs from 2005 to 2011: a Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 14 percent on banknote contracts and that the kickback returned to local decision makers. Prosecutors had told the court that former OeBS employees paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks in exchange for contracts to print money, an allegation as reported. OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Syrian official was named or tried. Syria appoints no private audit firm: article 68(3) of the same law gives the auditing of the bank's records and accounts to the Central Organization for Financial Control, the state's own supreme audit institution. A circulating 500-pound note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. Syria scores 40 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:SYR.current_paragraph: The Central Bank of Syria issues the Syrian pound, which moves within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Basic Monetary Law No. 23 of 2002, issued in Damascus on 17 March 2002 by President Bashar al-Assad, places the bank and its policy-making council under the government. Article 8(3) has its decisions passed to the Minister of Economy and Foreign Trade, who may suspend for up to seven days any decision he considers contrary to the interest of the state and must refer a continuing disagreement to the Council of Ministers. Article 69 has the Governor appointed, and his service ended, by decree; article 2 puts the Council's non-bank seats, among them assistant ministers and the head of the State Planning Authority, in the gift of a decree; and article 71 has the Minister name the four supervising directors who sit with the Governor on the management committee. Government pressure was reported in 11 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time pressing the bank to ease and demanding that it print money. One case runs from 2005 to 2011: a Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 14 percent on banknote contracts and that the kickback returned to local decision makers. Prosecutors had told the court that former OeBS employees paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks in exchange for contracts to print money, an allegation as reported. OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Syrian official was named or tried. Syria appoints no private audit firm: article 68(3) of the same law gives the auditing of the bank's records and accounts to the Central Organization for Financial Control, the state's own supreme audit institution. p:TON.box:
NATIONAL RESERVE BANK OF TONGA
Tonga
The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga, which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1 per cent or less against the US dollar. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12 in its 2020 revised edition, sets out how the government may steer it. Section 10(1) has the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, appoint five directors and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and section 11(1) has the Governor appointed by Cabinet on the Minister's recommendation. Section 50(1) lets the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, issue the bank written directives, and section 50(4) requires him to put any disagreement with the Board over a policy it has determined to Cabinet, which then determines the policy the bank adopts. The Governor is protected in office: under section 11(3) he may be removed by Cabinet, on the Minister's recommendation made at the Board's request, only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. Two cases are documented. In 2024 and 2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment, for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff, was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceedings, finding no reasonable cause of action. Between 2017 and 2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga; she pleaded guilty, her employment was terminated, and on 21 May 2019 the Supreme Court of Tonga gave her a two-year sentence, fully suspended, and ordered $800 compensation. Coopers & Lybrand audited the 1993 accounts, and De La Rue printed the 100-pa'anga note in the family introduced on 4 December 2023. One case is documented, and it is still under investigation: in late September 2026 an investigation in Santiago de Cuba concerned workers at two state banks, Banco Popular de Ahorro and BANDEC, both supervised by the Banco Central de Cuba, with reports saying the workers handed out cash in exchange for electronic transfers, charging commissions of between 30 and 50 per cent, acting together with self-employed people. Cash, banknote counting machines, magnetic cards and documents were reported seized, and no amounts, names or number of detainees were made public. The central bank's Minister-President, Juana Lilia Delgado Portal, issued an official note rejecting the conduct, ordering that any complaint be investigated without delay, and calling for administrative, labour and criminal responsibility to be established, internal controls strengthened and whistleblowers protected. On 12 April 2022 parliament approved President Ilham Aliyev's proposal to replace governor Elman Rustamov, in post since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank; Rustamov became adviser to the prime minister, and no official reason and no statement from him were reported.
